chunks: Bridge rectifier operation. The question: What is a bridge rectifier? How does it work?
A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond that turns AC into DC that only goes one way. The AC connects across two corners, and the load across the other two.
Whichever way the AC is pushing, two diodes steer the current through the load in the same direction.
Picture a pipe with water sloshing back and forth, and four one-way flap valves arranged so that, whichever way the water is pushed, it passes through a side chamber in the same direction.
The chamber is the load. The water still pulses, but it never reverses. That pulsing is the ripple, and a capacitor works as a small tank that smooths it.
Positive half-cycle. Terminal A is high.
Current (animated) leaves A, passes through D1 (green) to the positive rail, goes down through the capacitor and load, and returns through D4 (green) to terminal B.
D2 and D3 are reverse biased: D2 has B at its anode but the rail is higher.
Diode: a part that lets current through in only one direction. Half-cycle: half of one AC wave, either the positive or the negative half.
Peak voltage: the highest voltage of the AC wave. Reservoir capacitor: a capacitor that charges at the peaks and feeds the load between them.
Ripple: the leftover wiggle on the DC output.
Feed a 10 volts peak sine into a silicon bridge. Two diodes are in the path, each dropping about 0. 7 volts, so the output peaks at about 10 minus 1. 4 equals 8. 6 volts.
At 60 hertz, the output pulses 120 times per second, because both half-cycles now push the same way. That is the whole idea.
"A bridge rectifier is four diodes in a diamond: AC across one diagonal, load across the other.

On one half-cycle two diodes conduct and on the other half-cycle the other two do, but current always goes through the load in the same direction, so you get the absolute value of the input, pulsating DC at twice the line frequency.
Two diodes are in the path, so you lose about 1. 4 volts, and you add a capacitor to smooth it, with ripple of about I over 2fC."
